chunks: And the Sheikh — may God the Exalted support him — informed me, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn al-Walid, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn ʿAli ibn Mahbub al-Ashʿari, from Ahmad, from Ibrahim ibn Abi Mahmud,
who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about vomiting, nosebleed, and pus — do they nullify wudu or not? He said: «They do not nullify anything.»

key_terms.اَلرُّعَافِ: nosebleed (ru'af) — nasal hemorrhage; ruled not to nullify wudu
key_terms.اَلْقَيْءِ: vomiting (qay') — bodily discharge debated across schools; ruled here not to nullify wudu
key_terms.اَلْمِدَّةِ: pus (middah) — purulent wound discharge; ruled not to nullify wudu
key_terms.اَلْوُضُوءَ: wudu — ritual ablution required before salat and other acts of worship
key_terms.تَنْقُضُ: nullifies/breaks — juristic term for invalidating ritual purity (tahara)

ai.seo_question: Do vomiting, nosebleed, and pus invalidate wudu according to Imam al-Rida (AS) in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Ibrahim ibn Abi Mahmud, a companion of Imam al-Rida (AS), asks whether three bodily discharges — vomiting, nosebleed, and pus — invalidate wudu. The Imam rules unequivocally that none of them nullify wudu, reflecting the Imami Shia position that only acts expressly enumerated in the Quran (5:6) and authenticated Sunnah — such as urination, defecation, and flatulence — constitute true nullifiers of ritual purity.
